## Proof

**Claim:** Yes. If a discrete group $G$ admits a Følner sequence, then $G$ is countable.

**Setup.** Let $(F_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}$ be a Følner sequence for $G$. By definition, each $F_n$ is a finite, nonempty subset of $G$, and for every $g \in G$,
$$\frac{|gF_n \,\triangle\, F_n|}{|F_n|} \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$

**Key step.** Fix an arbitrary $g \in G$. Since left multiplication by $g$ is a bijection, $|gF_n| = |F_n|$. Hence
$$|gF_n \,\triangle\, F_n| \;=\; |gF_n| + |F_n| - 2\,|gF_n \cap F_n| \;=\; 2|F_n| - 2\,|gF_n \cap F_n|.$$

Dividing by $|F_n|$,
$$\frac{|gF_n \,\triangle\, F_n|}{|F_n|} \;=\; 2 - 2\,\frac{|gF_n \cap F_n|}{|F_n|}.$$

The Følner condition forces the left side to $0$, so
$$\frac{|gF_n \cap F_n|}{|F_n|} \;\longrightarrow\; 1.$$

In particular, for all sufficiently large $n$, $|gF_n \cap F_n| > 0$, i.e. $gF_n \cap F_n \neq \emptyset$.

**Extracting $g$ from the Følner sets.** Whenever $gF_n \cap F_n \neq \emptyset$, there exist $x, y \in F_n$ with $gx = y$, hence
$$g = y\,x^{-1} \in F_n\,F_n^{-1}.$$

So for every $g \in G$ there is an $N(g)$ such that $g \in F_n F_n^{-1}$ for all $n \geq N(g)$. Therefore
$$G \;\subseteq\; \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} F_n\,F_n^{-1}.$$

**Counting.** Each $F_n F_n^{-1}$ is finite (it has at most $|F_n|^2$ elements). The right-hand side is a countable union of finite sets, hence **countable**. Since $G$ is contained in a countable set, $G$ is countable. $\blacksquare$

**Remark.** This is exactly why, for uncountable discrete amenable groups, one must use Følner *nets* (indexed by arbitrary directed sets) rather than Følner *sequences*. A sequence is intrinsically countable, and the argument above shows it cannot "reach" every element of an uncountable group. The existence of a Følner sequence is therefore strictly stronger than amenability for uncountable groups; it is equivalent to amenability **plus countability**.
